children: More than 1,600 U.S. flights were canceled and nearly 3,600 delayed Sunday as airlines worked through a third day of disruption following Friday’s nationwide ground stop, according to FlightAware. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said operations should fully recover by Monday.
For investors, the disruption raises the prospect of lost airline revenue and higher costs from displaced passengers and crews. It also puts FAA contractor L3Harris
and could accelerate debate over billions of dollars in additional air traffic control spending, although the failure’s root cause remains unresolved.
canceled 27% of its Sunday flights and American Airlines
ranged from 3% to 5%. The problems followed more than 6,400 cancellations and 8,000 delays Saturday.
Officials linked the breakdown to a router installation by L3Harris

at an FAA facility in El Dorado, Arkansas. Duffy said that work triggered problems with another router in Amarillo, Texas, which flooded other control centers with data and disrupted communications. Friday’s resulting ground stop lasted almost five hours.

, Duffy said investigators had found no evidence of a cyberattack or deliberate sabotage. The FAA disabled the routers involved and roughly 60 similar devices while investigators continued examining the failure.

Duffy called for $50 billion to modernize air traffic control infrastructure, increasing his earlier $30 billion request. President Donald Trump also urged Congress to approve additional funding. The disruption has renewed concerns about aging equipment, communications failures and controller shortages.

House Democrats Rick Larsen and André Carson questioned the need for more funding, saying approximately $11 billion of the $12.5 billion approved in 2025 remained unspent. Duffy said the existing allocation covers specific projects and excludes new software needed to manage U.S. airspace.
